definition: Erratic means following no regular pattern — uneven and unpredictable in behavior or movement.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word erratic. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know erratic should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Doctors ordered a monitor after her pulse turned erratic, sprinting and slowing with no exertion to explain it.
Uneven is milder than erratic: an uneven pace merely varies, a little fast here and a little slow there, while an erratic one lurches, stalls, and races with no rhythm anyone could learn.
Chaotic goes further than erratic: erratic behavior still comes one surprise at a time from a single source, but chaos is every part of a system misfiring at once, with no thread left to follow.

Sporadic is about timing: sporadic events surface only now and then, with long gaps between — a few sightings a year, a cough that comes and goes. Erratic is about the behavior itself, uneven and lurching even while it is happening.

Haphazard points at the missing plan — a haphazard stack of boxes was thrown together with no care or system. Erratic describes the missing pattern in how something moves or performs; an erratic driver may be trying hard and swerving anyway.

Erratic means following no regular pattern — uneven and unpredictable in behavior or movement.

At the spring kite festival the wind turned erratic by noon: a long dead calm, then a gust out of the east that stood every kite on its tail, a shove from the north, calm again, two quick slaps from opposite quarters.
Fliers who had handled strong wind all their lives came down shaking their heads — strength they could work with; this had no rhythm to learn.
Erratic is the precise word because the wind's behavior held no pattern even while it blew — not weak, not rare, just lawless from minute to minute.
Sporadic wind would be something else entirely: a mostly still day broken by an occasional breeze, irregular only in when it shows up.
The erratic is patternless in how it acts; the sporadic is only scattered in when it appears.
Erratic is a chart-reader's word: it describes any motion, signal, or performance that follows no pattern — a heartbeat, a serve, a delivery schedule — and it passes no judgment on motive.
Its unit-mate capricious reads a mind into the swings, blaming whim and fancy; a faulty sensor is erratic, never capricious.
When the pattern is broken and no one chose the breaking, erratic is the exact word.

Ordonez threw nothing anyone could count on.
His knuckleball drifted, dived, or stalled — sometimes all three in one pitch — and radar guns disagreed with each other about it.
Catchers called his stuff erratic, and they meant it technically: the ball misbehaved continuously, in flight, not now and then between good innings.
Batting coaches gave up on film study.
A pattern you could learn was exactly what the pitch refused to supply.
Ordonez, for his part, insisted he aimed every throw.
The trying was real; the swerving came anyway.
He retired with the league's oddest line: few strikeouts, fewer solid hits.
